## Goal

Build idiomatic Go resilience primitives for backend services, inspired by the useful service-level ideas from `bluetape4k-resilience4j`.

## Direction

This milestone owns the `github.com/bluetape4k/bluetape-go/resilience` package as a first-party implementation.

- Provide composable policies similar in spirit to resilience4j/failsafe-go.
- Use external Go libraries only as reference material, not as runtime dependencies or wrappers.
- Keep the public API Go-native: `context.Context`, typed operations, explicit errors, deterministic tests, and small package boundaries.
- Prefer simple, inspectable implementations over broad framework behavior.

Reference-only inputs:

- `failsafe-go` for composable policy shape.
- `cenkalti/backoff` for retry delay and jitter design ideas.
- `sony/gobreaker` for circuit breaker state and half-open design ideas.
- `golang.org/x/sync/semaphore` for bulkhead design ideas.
- `golang.org/x/time/rate` for future rate limiter design ideas.

## Scope

- Composable policy core and function wrappers.
- Retry, timeout, circuit breaker, and bulkhead policies.
- Structured events/hooks for observability integration.
- HTTP middleware and examples for `net/http`.

Rate limiting remains a design reference for later milestones unless it is required by a concrete `0.2.0` child issue.

0.6.0 ports the first portable utility foundations from the bluetape4k ecosystem into idiomatic Go packages.

## Source parity target

Use the full bluetape4k ecosystem as source evidence, not only `bluetape4k-projects`:

- `bluetape4k-projects/utils/idgenerators`: UUID v1-v7, ULID, KSUID, Snowflake, GlobalSnowflake, Flake, Hashids, common generator interfaces, encoding helpers, and benchmarks.
- `bluetape4k-projects/utils/jwt`: JWT creation/parsing, provider/composer/reader model, KeyChain generation/rotation, distributed KeyChain repositories, compression, and clock/expiry helpers.
- `bluetape4k-projects/utils/measured`: type-safe `Measure`/`Units` model and units for length, time, mass, volume, temperature, angle, area, storage, binary size, frequency, energy, power, velocity, acceleration, graphics length, and pressure.
- `bluetape4k-projects/utils/money`: currency units, Money/FastMoney style amount models, decimal precision, rounding, exchange-rate conversion, aggregation, parsing, and serialization concerns.
- `bluetape4k-projects/utils/probabilistic`: dependency-free Bloom filter semantics, false-positive guarantees, merge compatibility, and concurrency caveats.

## 0.6.0 implementation scope

0.6.0 is the portable utilities foundation milestone, not full ecosystem parity for every utility family. Completion requires stable Go-native APIs, source-parity notes, and representative implementations that leave later expansion consistent.

0.6.0 includes:

- #32 ID generator common API and parity track.
- #164 UUID generator family.
- #165 ULID generator family.
- #167 Snowflake ID generator family.
- #33 JWT helper utilities.
- #34 measured values and units.
- #35 money and decimal helper research/adoption decision.
- #36 probabilistic Bloom filter support.

## Deferred scope

The following source-parity tracks are intentionally outside the 0.6.0 completion gate:

- #71 encryption/Tink facade: follow-up in milestone 0.7.0.
- #37 rule engine primitives: moved to milestone 0.13.0.
- #166 KSUID generator family: deferred until the common ID API and 0.6.0 UUID/ULID/Snowflake implementations are stable.
- Flake and Hashids: defer or split after Snowflake proves the numeric/compact ID API shape.

## Goal

Provide Go packages with similar user-facing capability where it is useful and safe in Go. Avoid mechanically cloning Kotlin APIs, but do not shrink issues to one narrow helper when the source library is a broader family. For 0.6.0 specifically, keep the release gate bounded to foundation-quality utilities that can be implemented, reviewed, documented, and stress-tested coherently.

## Acceptance criteria

- Each included utility issue records source parity target, Go-specific exclusions, dependency/adoption decision, and API consistency constraints.
- Public APIs are idiomatic Go and avoid Kotlin-shaped extension/DSL cloning unless the Go shape is still natural.
- Package READMEs include source-parity notes, selection guides where relevant, examples, and operational caveats.
- ID generator APIs are consistent across UUID, ULID, and Snowflake before later KSUID/Flake/Hashids work resumes.
- New code uses `GoroutineStressTester` and `AsyncJobTester` when concurrency, cancellation, or long-running behavior is part of the contract.

## Research: Go compressor candidates

### Recommended 0.1.0 scope

Use a small `compression` package with byte helpers and streaming `io.Reader`/`io.WriteCloser` support.

Standard-library algorithms:

- `gzip`: `compress/gzip`; broad compatibility and streaming read/write.
- `zlib`: `compress/zlib`; useful for zlib-format compatibility.
- `deflate`: `compress/flate`; raw DEFLATE when a container format is not wanted.

External direct dependencies:

- `zstd`: `github.com/klauspost/compress/zstd`; recommended default for general storage/transport because it balances speed and compression ratio in pure Go.
- `lz4`: `github.com/pierrec/lz4/v4`; good for fast internal cache/temp data and streaming support.
- `snappy`: `github.com/golang/snappy`; good for very fast low-ratio compression with framed stream support.

### Deferred candidates

- `bzip2`: Go stdlib only provides decompression; compression needs a separate dependency, so defer until a real compatibility need appears.
- `zip`: archive/container concern rather than a compressor primitive; defer to an archive/file package.
- `brotli`: possible via `github.com/andybalholm/brotli`, but mostly HTTP/static asset oriented and not needed for the 0.1.0 foundation.
- `s2`: possible via `github.com/klauspost/compress/s2`, but treat as a future performance-specialized option rather than a first foundation codec.

### Proposed contract

```go
type Compressor interface {
    Name() string
    Compress([]byte) ([]byte, error)
    Decompress([]byte) ([]byte, error)
    NewWriter(io.Writer) (io.WriteCloser, error)
    NewReader(io.Reader) (io.ReadCloser, error)
}
```

Default recommendation: use `zstd` for persisted service payloads, `gzip` for compatibility, and `lz4` or `snappy` for fast internal data.

Sources:

- https://pkg.go.dev/std
- https://github.com/klauspost/compress
- https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/pierrec/lz4/v4
- https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/golang/snappy
- https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/andybalholm/brotli

Port the `bluetape4k-idgenerators` family into a Go-native `id` package with a consistent API across generator algorithms.

## Source parity target

`bluetape4k-idgenerators` generates unique IDs in distributed environments using a variety of algorithms exposed through a unified `IdGenerator<T>` interface.

The Go package should provide a coherent family, not a one-off helper:

- UUID family: v4, v7, v6, and name/time-based variants where Go dependency support and privacy tradeoffs are acceptable.
- ULID family: random, monotonic, stateful monotonic, Crockford Base32 parse/format.
- Snowflake family: Snowflake/GlobalSnowflake-style numeric IDs, machine ID guidance, parse helpers, base36/string rendering, clock rollback errors.
- KSUID family: second precision and millisecond precision where feasible, Base62 parse/format.
- Flake and Hashids: source-parity candidates to split/defer unless their Go usefulness is confirmed after the common API is stable.
- Compact string helpers such as base62/base36 must be consistent across families.

## 0.6.0 implementation scope

0.6.0 validates the common API with the core families that are most useful for service code:

- #164 UUID generator family.
- #165 ULID generator family.
- #167 Snowflake ID generator family.

KSUID, Flake, and Hashids may remain tracked as source-parity candidates, but they are not required to close the 0.6.0 ID generator foundation unless they are explicitly pulled back into this milestone.

## API consistency requirement

Design the package around shared concepts before implementing individual algorithms:

- Small Go-native generator interfaces such as numeric/string/UUID generators, not Kotlin-shaped inheritance.
- Common naming for `Next`, `NextString`, `Parse`, `Must` avoidance, batch helpers, entropy/clock injection, and typed errors.
- A selection guide equivalent to the Kotlin README: DB primary key, request/correlation ID, URL-safe string ID, distributed machine ID, deterministic/name-based ID, and short obfuscated ID.
- Clear ordering and collision guarantees per algorithm.
- No algorithm-specific public API should make later UUID/ULID/KSUID/Snowflake integration inconsistent.

## Child implementation issues

This issue owns the common API/spec and tracks parity. Implementation is split to keep PRs reviewable:

- #164 UUID generator family.
- #165 ULID generator family.
- #166 KSUID generator family.
- #167 Snowflake ID generator family.

## Acceptance criteria

- Spec compares the full Kotlin algorithm set and chooses implement/split/defer for each family.
- Shared API is documented before family-specific implementation starts.
- Package README includes an algorithm selection guide similar to `bluetape4k-idgenerators`.
- 0.6.0 completion covers the common API plus UUID, ULID, and Snowflake unless the milestone scope is explicitly expanded.
- Each implemented family documents length, sortability, entropy source, collision scope, ordering guarantees, and parse/format behavior.
- Concurrency and collision tests use `GoroutineStressTester`.
- Async/cancellation-shaped tests use `AsyncJobTester` where generator options, batch helpers, or long-running paths can observe context/cancellation.

## Summary

Port `StrategicLeaderElector` from `bluetape4k-leader` to Go.

Instead of lock contention, uses a candidate-registry approach: nodes register themselves, apply a deterministic strategy to the same candidate list, and each node independently computes the winner.

## Kotlin Reference

- `leader-core`: `StrategicLeaderElector`, `ElectionStrategy`, `CandidateInfo`, `CandidateScorer`
- Strategies: `FifoElectionStrategy`, `RandomElectionStrategy`, `ScoredElectionStrategy`
- Scorers: `IdleTimeScorer`, `RecentSuccessScorer`, `SuccessRateScorer`, `WeightedScorer`

## Proposed Go API

```go
// leader/strategy.go
type CandidateInfo struct {
    NodeID       string
    RegisteredAt time.Time
    LastActiveAt time.Time
    SuccessCount int64
    FailureCount int64
    Weight       float64
}

type ElectionStrategy interface {
    Elect(candidates []CandidateInfo, nodeID string) (winner string)
}

type StrategicElector interface {
    RegisterCandidate(ctx context.Context, group string, info CandidateInfo, ttl time.Duration) error
    UnregisterCandidate(ctx context.Context, group string, nodeID string) error
    ListCandidates(ctx context.Context, group string) ([]CandidateInfo, error)
    UpdateResult(ctx context.Context, group string, nodeID string, success bool) error
    RunIfLeader(ctx context.Context, group string, strategy ElectionStrategy, action func() (any, error)) (any, error)
}
```

## Built-in Strategies

| Strategy | Description |
|---|---|
| `FifoStrategy` | Elects the earliest registered candidate |
| `RandomStrategy` | Random selection (seed-stable per round) |
| `ScoredStrategy` | Weighted score from pluggable scorers |

## Built-in Scorers (for ScoredStrategy)

| Scorer | Description |
|---|---|
| `IdleTimeScorer` | Prefers node idle the longest |
| `SuccessRateScorer` | Prefers node with highest success rate |
| `WeightedScorer` | Uses `CandidateInfo.Weight` directly |

## Candidate Registry Backend

Requires a shared store for candidate registration. Initial target: Redis (HSET with TTL per candidate key).

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `ElectionStrategy` interface and `CandidateInfo` type in `leader` package
- [ ] `StrategicElector` interface
- [ ] `FifoStrategy`, `RandomStrategy`, `ScoredStrategy` implementations
- [ ] `IdleTimeScorer`, `SuccessRateScorer`, `WeightedScorer`
- [ ] Redis-backed candidate registry in `leader/redis`
- [ ] Testcontainers-backed smoke tests
- [ ] Example: scored election for nightly job with idle-time preference

Evaluate whether bluetape-go should provide a Redis server-assisted near-cache implementation based on RESP3 `CLIENT TRACKING` as a first-class alternative to application-level Pub/Sub invalidation.

## Background

Issue #23 will implement the first near-cache invalidation strategy with an application-level Redis Pub/Sub protocol. That satisfies the immediate acceptance criteria, but Redis also provides server-assisted client-side caching through `CLIENT TRACKING`. The RESP3 strategy has different lifecycle, connection, and invalidation semantics, so it should be evaluated as a separate near-cache strategy rather than hidden behind the Pub/Sub implementation.

## Research summary

- App-level Pub/Sub invalidation is controlled by bluetape-go. It can publish namespace, operation, key, origin ID, and protocol version in a stable invalidation message.
- RESP3 `CLIENT TRACKING` is server-assisted. Redis tracks keys read by a client connection and sends invalidation when another client modifies those keys.
- Redis `CLIENT TRACKING` supports options such as `BCAST`, `PREFIX`, `OPTIN`, `OPTOUT`, and `NOLOOP`. These options should be modeled explicitly if supported.
- RESP3 tracking can catch external Redis writes that do not route through bluetape-go, but connection lifecycle and push-message handling are more complex than ordinary Pub/Sub.
- Managed Redis and Redis proxy RESP3 support must be verified before documenting this as a production-ready strategy.

## Acceptance criteria

- Document whether `go-redis/v9` can support a robust `CLIENT TRACKING` implementation without replacing the Redis dependency.
- Decide the public constructor/API shape, for example a future `redisnear.NewTracking(...)` strategy.
- Verify the required Redis server version and managed Redis compatibility assumptions.
- Define disconnect/reconnect behavior, including local cache flush and tracking re-enable policy.
- Define how `NOLOOP` and external writes interact with cache-aside or write-through flows.
- Add or plan a Testcontainers proof where an external Redis write invalidates a tracked local entry.

## Source links

- Redis client-side caching introduction: https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/clients/client-side-caching/
- Redis `CLIENT TRACKING`: https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/client-tracking/
- Redis client-side caching reference: https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/client-side-caching/
- go-redis repository: https://github.com/redis/go-redis

- #23 implements the first Pub/Sub near-cache strategy.
- Research PR: #111
- Research document path: `docs/superpowers/research/2026-06-04-issue-23-near-cache-invalidation-strategies.md`

## Problem

The v0.5.0 `batch` package can advance a checkpoint after a failed writer chunk is skipped, even though the `Writer` contract does not require chunk writes to be atomic or idempotent.

`Step.flush` calls `s.write(...)`; when that returns an error and `SkipPolicy` accepts it, the current code increments `SkipCount` by the full chunk cost and immediately calls `saveCheckpoint(ctx)`. That checkpoint comes from the reader after the whole chunk has already been read, so a restart resumes after every item in the chunk.

## Evidence

- `batch/step.go:189-193`: failed writer chunks are skipped and `saveCheckpoint(ctx)` is called.
- `batch/step.go:248-260`: checkpoints are saved from the reader's current progress.
- `batch/interfaces.go:38-42`: `Writer.Write` has no atomic/idempotent/partial-write contract.
- `leader/redis/coordination_example_test.go:433-438`: the example Redis list writer writes items one by one and returns on the first `RPush` failure, which demonstrates a non-atomic writer shape.
- Current tests cover writer failure counts and restart after hard writer failure, but do not cover partial writer side effects followed by skip+checkpoint.

## Impact

If a writer persists part of a chunk and then returns an error, `SkipPolicy` can mark the whole chunk as skipped and persist a checkpoint beyond it. On restart, unwritten items in that chunk are not retried. Already-written items may also be misreported as skipped. This is a data-loss / duplicate-accounting risk for the public batch API when users combine chunk writers, skip policy, and checkpoint restart.

## Suggested direction

- Make writer-skip checkpointing safe by either:
  - requiring/documenting atomic or idempotent chunk writers before checkpoint advancement, or
  - disabling checkpoint advancement for skipped writer chunks unless the writer reports a committed boundary, or
  - splitting writer skip semantics so item-level processor skips can advance checkpoints but chunk writer failures cannot silently advance durable progress.
- Add a regression test with a writer that writes the first item in a chunk, returns an error, `SkipPolicy` accepts the error, and a second run proves no item is silently lost or misreported.

## Review source

Found during a 7-Tier review of the v0.5.0 milestone diff (`v0.4.0..v0.5.0`).

P0=0 P1=1 for the review gate; this issue records the P1 finding.

## Context

Issue #166 is scoped to standard seconds-precision KSUID support for the `id` package. During spec review, millisecond-precision KSUID was split out because it is not safely interchangeable with standard Segment KSUID.

bluetape4k Kotlin source provides `Ksuid.Millis` using a 20-byte layout with 8-byte millisecond timestamp plus 12-byte payload, rendered as a 27-character Base62 string through a custom `BytesBase62` alphabet/bit-stream encoder. Segment KSUID uses a different standard seconds layout and Base62 encoding.

## Problem

A bare 27-character Base62 string does not identify whether it is standard seconds KSUID or bluetape4k millis KSUID. A seconds parser can silently reinterpret a millis string and return the wrong timestamp, and vice versa.

## Scope

- Decide whether bluetape-go should implement KSUID millis at all.
- If implemented, choose one explicit compatibility contract:
  - exact Kotlin `Ksuid.Millis` string compatibility,
  - a distinguishable bluetape-go representation, or
  - a documented non-compatible Segment-alphabet variant.
- Define parse/time APIs that cannot silently reinterpret standard seconds KSUID values as millis values without documented behavior.
- Add deterministic cross-language/vector tests if exact Kotlin compatibility is selected.
- Update `id` README files and selection guidance.

## Non-goals

- Do not block #166 standard KSUID seconds support.
- Do not change UUID, ULID, or Snowflake APIs.
- Do not claim strict monotonicity unless the implementation proves it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Compatibility decision is documented with evidence from Kotlin source and Go dependency source.
- API shape avoids silent cross-family timestamp misinterpretation or documents it as an explicit accepted behavior.
- Tests cover canonical encoding, decoding, timestamp extraction, invalid strings, cross-family parse behavior, goroutine uniqueness, and race safety.
- Documentation clearly distinguishes Segment-compatible KSUID seconds from any millis variant.

## Background

The normalized ID generator benchmark snapshot in PR #191 shows that Go is not
currently faster than Kotlin for several string ID families:

- UUID v4
- UUID v7
- ULID in some single-thread comparisons
- KSUID seconds
- KSUID milliseconds

This issue tracks a Go-side investigation and optimization pass for those
generators. The goal is to separate real implementation cost from benchmark
shape differences.

## Scope

- Profile UUID v4, UUID v7, random ULID, monotonic ULID, KSUID, and KSUID millis
  generation.
- For UUID, compare the current convenience-function benchmark against a
  reused-generator benchmark, because `NewUUIDV4()` and `NewUUIDV7()` currently
  create a generator per operation.
- For ULID, compare random vs monotonic paths explicitly. Kotlin's
  `UlidGenerator` uses a stateful monotonic path, while Go reports random and
  monotonic rows separately.
- Separate entropy cost, byte construction, timestamp access,
  string formatting/encoding, synchronization, and allocation cost.
- Compare per-call string-return APIs against lower-level byte/value or
  reusable-buffer paths where appropriate.
- Check whether generator reuse, timestamp caching, entropy buffering, or
  encoding changes can reduce latency and allocations without weakening
  correctness.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Fresh `go test -bench` baseline is recorded with `benchmem`, command,
  environment, and raw output.
- Benchmark rows include:
  - UUID convenience functions vs reused UUID generators.
  - ULID random vs ULID monotonic, both single-thread and parallel.
  - KSUID seconds vs KSUID millis, both single-thread and parallel.
- CPU and allocation profiles identify the dominant cost for each target
  generator.
- Before/after results are compared with `benchstat` or an equivalent
  normalized table using one unit such as `ns/id`.
- Any optimization keeps existing API behavior and correctness guarantees.
- Concurrency-sensitive changes include bounded stress coverage and
  `go test -race`.
- Benchmark docs explain whether the measurement includes string encoding,
  allocation, entropy, and generator construction.

## Notes

- PR #191 indicates Go Snowflake is very fast, but string-oriented UUID, ULID,
  and KSUID paths may spend most of their time in entropy, formatting, encoding,
  synchronization, and allocation rather than in simple arithmetic.
- Go UUID results are especially suspect as a pure hot-path comparison because
  the current benchmark calls `NewUUIDV4()` / `NewUUIDV7()`, which construct a
  generator per ID.
- ULID should not be judged from a random-vs-monotonic mismatch. Kotlin's
  `UlidGenerator` is stateful monotonic; Go has separate random and monotonic
  benchmark rows.
- Treat this as an implementation-level optimization target, not as a language
  ranking.
